title: Benefits and harms of antihypertensive treatment in low-risk patients with mild hypertension
authors: Sheppard JP, Stevens S, Stevens R, Martin U, Mant J, Hobbs FDR, et al.
population: Patients aged 18 to 74 years in the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink, 1998 to 2015, with untreated mild hypertension (140/90 to 159/99 mm Hg) and no cardiovascular disease or risk factors; 19,143 treated within 12 months of diagnosis matched by propensity score to 19,143 untreated
funder: This work was funded by Medical Research Council (MRC) Strategic Skills Postdoctoral Fellowship MR/K022032/1 (Dr Sheppard), a National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) professorship (Dr Sheppard and Mr McManus), and grant NIHR-RP-R2-12-015 from the NIHR, with further NIHR support. The funding sources had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; and decision to submit the manuscript for publication.
authorConflicts: R. Stevens is a member of the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Independent Scientific Advisory Committee but was not involved in approving the study; no other disclosures.
result: Treatment was not associated with mortality (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.17) or cardiovascular disease (1.09, 0.95 to 1.25). It was associated with hypotension (1.69, 1.30 to 2.20; number needed to harm over 10 years 41), syncope (1.28, 1.10 to 1.50; 35), electrolyte abnormalities (1.72, 1.12 to 2.65; 111) and acute kidney injury (1.37, 1.00 to 1.88; 91). The authors advise caution in generalising trial findings in high-risk individuals to people at lower risk.
